d433bf50-3272-569f-a940-5a05965ceb20.name: Marble cenotaphs.
d433bf50-3272-569f-a940-5a05965ceb20.description:
No. 2536 is a covered cenotaph in the shape of a rectangular prism. The marble is carved in relief. The side panels, the cover, and tombstones at either end were prepared individually, and then assembled by slotting them together along open grooves.  
  
The tombstone panels at either end of the cenotaph are crowned with large palmette-leaf motifs and have columns on both sides. The bodies of the columns are decorated with *mihrab*\-niches with *muqarnas* hoods, while their tops end in grooved knobs. The front and back faces of the palmette leaves are filled with vegetal compositions with palmette motifs, carved in shallow relief. The tombstone has a four-line inscription in *thuluth*\-style calligraphy which begins at the bottom of the palmette motif and terminates with another palmette-leaf motif at its lower end. The lower edges of the tombstone are shaped like grooved colonnettes with zigzag motifs. The cenotaph's side-faces feature an Arabic inscription in *thuluth*\-style calligraphy framed in cartouches with rectangular lotus-and-palmette borders. On the bevelled side-borders of the cenotaph cover is a frieze consisting of a series of palmettes. On top of the cover, a motif of a lamp with a body in the shape of a six-lobed medallion is shown as if hanging from a chain. This motif is used quite frequently in Anatolian gravestones, symbolically representing the illumination of the deceased person's path to God.  
  
According to the inscription, the cenotaph belongs to the wife of özdemir, the governor of Aleppo. She died in Safar 893 / AD January–February 1488.  
  
No. 2537: The material, shape and details of ornament, except for some very small differences of surface decoration, are similar to those of cenotaph no. 2536.  
  
The cover-slab of this cenotaph is decorated with a geometric network filled with split-palmette motifs as well as a water-reservoir to collect rainwater, from which birds can take a drink, in the form of a lobed rosette. The inscription says that the cenotaph belongs to the governor of Aleppo, özdemir, who died in Safar 899 (AD November–December 1493).
d433bf50-3272-569f-a940-5a05965ceb20.short_description: These two marble cenotaphs belonged to the Mamluk governor of Aleppo, Özdemir, and his wife according to their inscriptions. They were brought from the mausoleum of Özdemir at Ansariyya near Aleppo and stand out with their rich geometric and floral decoration.

In addition, Herzfeld (1956) documents that according to the inscription on özdemir's tomb, it was completed by an architect named Yusuf ibn al-Kamal in Rabi' I 893 (February–March 1488).
d433bf50-3272-569f-a940-5a05965ceb20.method_for_provenance: According to inventory documents, the cenotaphs were taken from özdemir's tomb in Ansariyya, near Aleppo in and brought to the Museum. For this reason it is probable that they were made in Aleppo or its vicinity.

The objects were transferred to the Museum in 1941.

e27dbed9-8298-54dd-abc1-a2b737a79abc.name: Tombstone.
e27dbed9-8298-54dd-abc1-a2b737a79abc.description:
A rectangular stone which combines decorative beauty with the epigraphic scheme in a remarkable way. It is designed along architectural lines, with a 'symbolic' arch of interlaced lobes, above which is a band of Islamic merlons (the alternating raised parts of a parapet). Inside the arch, a lively cursive script is interlaced with arabesques. In the spaces between the columns, in a narrow rectangular frame, are three lines in a script remarkably distinctive for its long vertical lines and the elongation of its final letters.  
The famous Arabist Frei João de Sousa referred to it for the first time in 1788, as visible on one of the outer walls of the Town Hall at Évora, although it was seen shortly afterwards by English architect James Murphy, and referred to in his publication of 1795, *Travels in Portugal*. The fact that the object was found broken and somewhat worn away, as well as the inadequate drawing by Murphy, made it hard to read the sentence inscribed in the arch until quite recently. The full reading was only put forward for the first time in 1940 by A. R. Nykl, although with some reservations because of the difficulty of reading the final two lines, and is as follows:  
'All souls shall experience death (Qur'an, III, 182). You who visit \[this tomb\], ask God to forgive your brother and have mercy on him and remember this journey \[to the Last Judgement\]. \[The soul\] shall be taken from you by God; no vestige of his pride appears in the humble tomb. From the injustice \[of this world\] we must return to the Lord; that is to say, to God, in his Mercy and great Generosity.'
e27dbed9-8298-54dd-abc1-a2b737a79abc.short_description: This tombstone was commissioned by Muslims who had stayed in Évora following the reconquest of the town. The text cites the Qur'an (III, 182) in a piece that elegantly combines architectural elements (a crenellated lobed arch) and a cursive text with arabesques.
e27dbed9-8298-54dd-abc1-a2b737a79abc.dimensions: Height 35 cm, width 49 cm, depth 4.5 cm.
e27dbed9-8298-54dd-abc1-a2b737a79abc.method_for_datation: The stylistic and epigraphic characteristics date from 7th / 13th century.

e3ee67e9-9290-5553-9312-7583df9e2ebd.name: Funerary stele.
e3ee67e9-9290-5553-9312-7583df9e2ebd.description:
Funerary stele, broken into two parts, featuring an inscription in flowery *kufic* calligraphy, engraved concavely. The text consists of three lines that specify:  
\- \[In the name of Allah, the Clement, the Merciful, may the salvation of\] Allah be upon Muhammad and his family … This …  
\- al-Tamimi, died the day \[Monday? Sunday? Wednesday?\]  
\- …four hundred and thirteen \[AD 1022\].
e3ee67e9-9290-5553-9312-7583df9e2ebd.short_description: Funerary stele from Achir, broken into two pieces. An engraved inscription in *kufic* characters gives the name of the deceased and the date of death.

e3ee67e9-9290-5553-9312-7583df9e2ebd.method_for_datation: In his reproduction of the text, Marçais highlighted the restoration/repair work, which looks as if it was done following the form of the letters.

e78c6ccf-a931-5f61-a53f-9a33b0ed0065.name: Sepulchral stele.
e78c6ccf-a931-5f61-a53f-9a33b0ed0065.description: The stele has a shaped base decorated with an elegant frieze with plant volutes in a style exemplified by the funerary stelae of Palermo. Both edges have been damaged. The Arabic script is in elongated *kufic* characters in the Fatimid style. According to M. Amari (see Bibliography), it reads: ‘ In the name of God the compassionate … give peace. Each soul must savour its own ability, because the day of resurrection (now) whoever misses hell, barely, and makes it to Paradise, has attained a great triumph. The life of this world … illusion. The power … Prophet. This is the tomb of Ayyub (son of …) Mukhallaf, the fuller, who died on Saturday in the first ten days of Rajab of the year five hundred and seventeen \[25 August to 3 September 1123\]. God have mercy on him’. The textile industry was very widespread in Sicily, as attested by another inscription from AH 462 / AD 1072 still kept at the Regional Gallery of Sicily (San Giovanni list no. 61), which mentions Ibrahim, a *dibag* (silk cloth) weaver.
e78c6ccf-a931-5f61-a53f-9a33b0ed0065.short_description: Tomb with *kufic* inscriptions. Tombs and stelae often bore formulas taken from the Qur’an, sometimes with expressions of the virtues of the deceased. In this case, the dead man’s trade is mentioned (weaver), evidence of the vitality of textile production by Muslim craftsmen in Sicily at that time.

ee7b7bd6-50bf-52d7-91be-0e545a0d41c3.name: Sarcophagus of Count Emerik Erdödy
ee7b7bd6-50bf-52d7-91be-0e545a0d41c3.description:
The sarcophagus-shaped pewter casket of Count Emerik Erdödy – in the crypt of the side chapel of St. Anthony of Padua in the Franciscan Church in Klanjec – rests on the backs of four stags placed at each corner, with two outspread-winged eagles withholding the weight of the central part. On the front is the coat-of-arms of Emerik Erdödy. At each side, lace-like ornamentation surrounds a cartouche in relief, with an inscription, lion's heads with rings, and skull and crossbones.  
In design and iconography, the sarcophagus shows the mature Baroque spirit expressed through the splendid workmanship and vivid imagination of the master who made it.  
The skull and crossbones motif was used as a symbol of transience and a reminder of the emptiness of earthly matters.  
Iconographically, the stag symbolises pious solitude, a pure life, and the Eucharist but here the stag is purely decorative. This is probably because it was a device used in Erdödy's coat of arms, and Emerik's nephews – having commissioned the sarcophagus – may have thought it fitting to use the stag whose large antlers, with seven points, may symbolise the seven decades of Emerik's life.  
The use of animal figures taken from a family's coat of arms was common, and they appear often as the casket bearers of the deceased. For example, two-headed, outstretched-winged eagles carry the sarcophagus of Empress Margarita Theresa Habsburg (Capuchin crypt in Vienna), a heraldic motif that appears on the Habsburg coat of arms. Furthermore, eagles were a common feature of funereal architecture at the turn of the 17th century.  
Emerik's sarcophagus has many features in common with the Habsburg sarcophagi in the Capuchin crypt.  
It was usual for prominent people to have ceremonial funerals, from the setting of the rite to the appearance of the tomb. Modelling themselves on the imperial family, the families of magnates followed this trend, as seen here in the Erdödy sarcophagus. Its ornate appearance – with emphasis on the decorative effects placed *inside* the tomb – was a reflection of the family's great wealth. Erdödy's close cultural link with Vienna the capital, is expressed in the design and motifs of the sarcophagus attributed to the circle of the renowned 17th-century Viennese pewterers, very probably Johann Philipp Stumpf, who was the designer for Empress Eleonora Maria's (d. 1697) sarcophagus, which rests on four lions.
ee7b7bd6-50bf-52d7-91be-0e545a0d41c3.short_description:
The sarcophagus of Count Emerik Erdödy, (d. 1690), rests on the backs of four sitting stags in the crypt of the side chapel of St. Anthony of Padua in the Franciscan Church in Klanjec, which the Croatian branch of the Erdödys built in the 17th century.  
The design of the sarcophagus with sitting stags is unique, but there is a degree of an analogy with Empress Eleonora Maria’s (d. 1697) sarcophagus, which, similarly, rests on the figures of four lions, and which the Viennese pewterer, Johann Philipp Stumpf designed.

ef74c9ed-a4dc-57df-a3a1-c5538d838390.name: *Tomb statue of Prince Pál Esterházy and his first wife (Orsolya Esterházy?)*
ef74c9ed-a4dc-57df-a3a1-c5538d838390.description:
The four wooden statues representing the Esterházy brothers (Pál and Ferenc) and their wives were certainly commissioned by the Pál Esterházy family. The founder of the dynasty, Palatin Pál, built a family mausoleum in the Franciscan Church in Kismarton (Eisenstadt), within the residential area that formed part of his large estates. Although the crypt was completely rebuilt in 1856–57 its previous appearance can be reconstructed on the basis of a detailed description of the interior from 1835–36 and a plan of the building. As these documents prove, the Kismarton (Eisenstadt) Mausoleum consisted of a lower and an upper chapel. The rounded niches on the upper level were for the gilded-wood, kneeling figures of Pál and Ferenc Esterházy, Orsolya Esterházy and Kata Thököly. The statues in the Hungarian National Gallery, one of which also bears some marks of gilding, seem to be identical to these niche figures. The statues are composed on a frontal view. Their backs are grooved, and their feet are not perfectly carved, a sign that the statues were designed for wall-niches. Pál Esterházy is represented in somewhat historic clothes (coat-of-arms and a short skirt), with a wig, and the Order of the Golden Fleece, which he obtained in 1681. His wife wears Hungarian apparel, a shoulder corset decorated with flowers, a blouse with pleated shoulders, a girdle decorated with precious stones and a necklace.  
In the lower chapel is the still extant sarcophagus of Palatin Pál, which could be viewed from the upper level through the lattice window. There was an altar dedicated to the Virgin Mary in each chapel. Members of the Esterházy family kneeling in the niches of the upper chapel in gestures of eternal worship were, thus, turned to the Virgin Mary mourning her son, suggesting therefore that they committed themselves to her patronage not only in life but even in death.  
The design of Pál Esterházy's sepulchral chapel represents an organic part of his art patronage, in which the cult of the Virgin Mary was determinative.
ef74c9ed-a4dc-57df-a3a1-c5538d838390.short_description: The sculptures represent the founder of the Esterházy dynasty, Pál Esterházy, and his first wife, Orsolya Esterházy (together with the figures of his brother and sister-in-law) kneeling in prayer. The works originate from the Kismarton (Eisenstadt) family vault and are representative examples of 17th-century portrait sculpture of the region.

f076e01a-b92e-50ef-8e77-6d8f18842351.name: Fragmentary cenotaph cover with Qur'anic calligraphy
f076e01a-b92e-50ef-8e77-6d8f18842351.short_description: This rectangular silk textile exhibits a design of chevron bands containing calligraphic inscriptions in *thuluth* script with verses of the Qur’an, invocations to God, and the *shahada*, or Muslim profession of faith. f6ae32d0-26a3-5232-9705-0322c2eb9e64.name: Funerary stele fragment.
f6ae32d0-26a3-5232-9705-0322c2eb9e64.description: A fragment from a funerary stele, nearly square in shape, the lower portion of which is broken off. In the centre are four lines of foliated *kufic* script, with the remains of a fifth line below them, framed by a narrow split-palmette scroll-band. The first line of the inscription reads ‘Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim …’ (‘In the Name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful…’), a standard *bismillah* that is normally followed by the name of the deceased and the date, although the continuation of this text has not been fully deciphered. Although orthodox Islam prohibits the marking of graves, most Islamic societies disregarded this rule, and in a Shi’ite context in particular, it was usual to mark a grave with a funerary *stele*.
f6ae32d0-26a3-5232-9705-0322c2eb9e64.short_description: In Islam the marking of graves is frowned upon, but gravestone fragments like this one show that many Muslims disregarded this. Generally grave markers started with the *bismillah*, ‘In the Name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful … ’, then named the deceased and gave the date of their death.
f6ae32d0-26a3-5232-9705-0322c2eb9e64.method_for_datation: The style of *kufic* script employed on this funerary stele with characteristic swan-necked ascenders, complies with Fatimid epigraphy dating to the late 4th– 5th / 11th century.
f6ae32d0-26a3-5232-9705-0322c2eb9e64.method_for_provenance: This fragment displays a typical example of Fatimid epigraphy from Egypt.
f6ae32d0-26a3-5232-9705-0322c2eb9e64.obtention: A gift from the Trustees of Surgeon Major General S. A. Lithgow of Fanhope in 1936.

f78b2e38-75a4-536e-b940-646dcbc84e4e.name: *Ash-shahadatan* (Declaration of Faith)
f78b2e38-75a4-536e-b940-646dcbc84e4e.short_description:
The most basic requirement of being a Muslim is to publicly declare one’s faith, in Arabic, with sincerity and without reservation. The Declaration of Faith is one of the five pillars of Islam and provides a foundation for all other Islamic beliefs and practices. In translation, it usually reads, "There is no God but Allah and Muhammed is His Messenger." This tombstone has the Muslim Declaration of Faith carved in Arabic on one face of it.  
  
The following are the critical conditions of the Declaration of Faith:  
1\. *al-‘Ilm* - Knowledge of the meaning of the *shahadatan* (the inscription of faith in the religion of Islam), its negation and affirmation.  
2\. *al-Yaqin* - Certainty; perfect knowledge of it that counteracts suspicion and doubt.  
3\. *al-Inqiyad* - Submission to its rightful requirements, which are the duties that must be performed with sincerity to God (alone).  
4\. *al-Qubul* - Acceptance that contradicts rejection.  
5\. *al-Ikhlas* - Sincerity, to negate polytheism.  
6\. *al-Sidq* - Truthfulness; that permits neither falsehood nor hypocrisy.  
7\. *al-Mahabbah* -Love of the *shahadatan* and its meaning.
f78b2e38-75a4-536e-b940-646dcbc84e4e.obtention: Ministry of Heritage and Culture Collection
keywords: Declaration of Faith; Tombstone

fed4821c-aab3-5f04-9bef-3b13115970a7.name: Funerary stele (gravestone).
fed4821c-aab3-5f04-9bef-3b13115970a7.description:
A square marble plaque with moulded borders framing and separating twin epitaphs, each composed of nine lines of *kufic* script carved in relief. The characters are carefully and elegantly carved and the groove etched on each one underlines its graceful contours. The alphabet is chosen from a classical type which uses chamfered uprights and furls containing stylised fleurons.  
Left epitaph:  
'*Basmala, tasliyah*. Muhammad died on the Thursday of the last decade of *Rabi* *al-awwal* \[first month\], in the year 480 \[1087\], bearing witness to the oneness of God'.  
Right epitaph:  
'*Basmala, tasliyah*. Abd al-Azim son of Abd Allah al-Tanuhi al-Zayyat died on the Friday of the last decade of the last *rabi* month, in the year 495 \[1101\], bearing witness to the oneness of God'.  
The latter man is probably the son, brother or father of Muhammad. Only the forenames are mentioned since he would be identified by the main epitaph.
fed4821c-aab3-5f04-9bef-3b13115970a7.short_description: Piece in the form of a square marble plaque with moulded edges framing and separating twin nine-line epitaphs in *kufic* script in relief. The inscription is neat and refers to two people.
fed4821c-aab3-5f04-9bef-3b13115970a7.method_for_datation: The epitaph has two dates. It was clearly carved after the death of the second man in 495 (1101).
fed4821c-aab3-5f04-9bef-3b13115970a7.method_for_provenance: The stele, which was found in the Zawiya of Sidi ‘Abd al-Azim, was carved in memory of the man described in the right-hand epitaph that has the same name and seems to have been venerated by the Tunisians.
fed4821c-aab3-5f04-9bef-3b13115970a7.obtention: After the demolition of the Zawiya Sidi ‘Abd al-Azim in the 1950s, the stele went to the Sidi Bu Khrissan Mausoleum in Tunis. It has been on display at the Sidi Qasim al-Jallizi Museum since 1978.
